# Karpathy guidelines — behavioral rules against common LLM coding mistakes

Curated by Skill Harbor — @multica-ai's behavioral guidelines for agents, derived from Andrej Karpathy's observations on how LLM-written code goes wrong. Four rules: think before coding (state assumptions explicitly, surface tradeoffs, push back when a simpler approach exists, ask instead of hiding confusion), simplicity first (minimum code that solves the problem — no speculative features, single-use abstractions, unrequested configurability, or impossible-scenario error handling; "if you write 200 lines and it could be 50, rewrite it"), surgical changes (touch only what the request requires, match existing style, mention unrelated dead code instead of deleting it, clean up only the orphans your own changes created), and goal-driven execution (transform tasks into verifiable success criteria and loop until verified — "add validation" becomes "write tests for invalid inputs, then make them pass"). MIT-licensed per the skill's frontmatter (note: the repo manifest declares no license — see caveat). Honest caveats: the guidelines bias toward caution over speed, so use judgment on trivial tasks; the tradeoff list is explicitly about coding agents, not a general writing style; license stated as MIT in the SKILL.md frontmatter while the repository manifest shows none — confirm before redistributing. Skill Harbor never reviews the code, review it yourself before use. Discovered via skills.sh.
